1:
What the healing was divides them. Gill will not have it a wish, nor a bare attempt made by the admonitions of the prophets, but an actual healing, and a political one: the restoring of their civil state in the days of Jeroboam the son of Joash, who recovered the coast of Israel from the entering of Hamath to the sea of the plain. Ellicott would translate it as present, When I heal Israel, and takes it of a lull in the attacks of the menacing foe, or of a thrill of finer feeling such as one recorded act of mercy to captives. Henry takes it of the whole offer: their disease was likely to be fatal, but God offered to be their physician, and would both have reformed them by his laws and prophets and delivered them from their troubles; their declining state seemed sometimes in a hopeful way of recovery, but their own folly put them back. If souls perish in their sin, he adds, the blame is not on God.

Calvin and Henry explain the discovery by the treatment. Calvin compares God to a physician who, wishing to try remedies, finds hidden and worse diseases: a sick man’s complaint is soon discovered, but he may have laboured for years under maladies that do not come at once to the physician’s knowledge. So God, by applying remedies, found how corrupt Israel was, and the iniquities of Samaria proved not common but inveterate. They might have pleaded that no nation under the sun is free of the common diseases; the answer is that they were too far gone for light remedies. Henry puts it as surgery: as a surgeon probes a wound to cure it and finds it touches the vitals, so God came down to see their case with kind intentions and found their wickedness so flagrant, and them so impenitent, that he could not in honour show the favour he designed.

That vice grows worse under treatment is their next point. Henry says that when endeavours were used to reform them the wickedness that had been restrained broke out, and swelled higher as a stream does when dammed. Calvin makes it a rule: men who disguise themselves gain nothing, for their hidden vices come to light at last, especially when the Lord performs the office of a physician. Where God does not try men, and there is no teaching that cauterizes or draws blood, they rest quietly in their own dregs and their perverseness never appears; but where he puts forth the power of his word, men show what impiety was hidden in them and rise up in rage.

Calvin takes Samaria for the capital and chief seat of government, and Ellicott says it stands to Israel as Jerusalem does to Judah, the source of the corruption of the country.

The second verse names what they never did. Gill follows the original, that they did not say to their hearts: they never put it to their consciences that the Lord saw all their actions and set them down in the book of his remembrance, to call them to account. Calvin traces the contempt of God to this root, that men imagine him as it were sleeping in heaven; they dare not deny him, yet take from him what belongs to his divinity by excluding him from the office of judge, and allow themselves any liberty, as though they had made a truce with him. Nothing, he says, ought to be more feared than being so fascinated as to think God rests idly in heaven. Clarke says they know not their own evil doings to be as a host of enemies encompassing them; Wesley adds that the doings are their own, not their fathers, as the incorrigible complain, and beset them as an enemy invests a town; Ellicott says the deeds crowded around as witnesses of their treason.
3:
Whose gladness it is comes first. Gill fixes on no one king but takes the kings in succession, who were delighted with the priests offering sacrifice to the calves and with the people attending that worship, by which they hoped to secure the kingdom and keep the people from going up to Jerusalem; it made them glad to the heart to hear that God was as well pleased with sacrifices at Dan and Bethel as at Jerusalem. Clarke says the people pleased the king by coming readily into his measures and joining heartily in his idolatry, professing to be perfectly happy in the change and greatly advantaged by their new gods. Ellicott turns it round: the evil awakens no alarm but rather sympathy and gladness in their kings and rulers, who are ready to follow suit in all deeds of violence. Wesley puts the initiative with the court, whose courtiers make it their work to invent pleasing wickedness and acquaint the king with it, the lies being false accusations against the innocent.

Calvin will not let the blame rest on the throne. It might have seemed worthy of praise that the people quietly embraced what the king commanded, and many in his own day bring that pretext forward; but he has already condemned this sort of obedience, and here shows that the defection is not to be ascribed to the king or to a few men, being a common evil that involved all in one guilt. If they wish to cast the blame on their governors it will be done in vain. Whence came such promptitude? As soon as Jeroboam formed the calves and built the temples, religion collapsed and whatever had been pure degenerated. Because the people had inwardly concocted their wickedness, it showed itself as soon as an occasion was offered; hypocrisy lay hid in them all, and was then discovered.

From this Calvin draws a rule about nations. A vice often creeps in that proceeds from one man or a few; but when all readily embrace what a few introduce, it is evident they have no living root of piety. Under a prudent and pious magistrate a people will give some hope of fearing the Lord; when an ungodly ruler succeeds, the greater part fall back at once.

The adultery is of both kinds. Gill takes it of king, princes, priests and people, in a spiritual and a bodily sense together: they were all idolaters, eager of it and constant in it, and addicted also to bodily adultery, a prevailing vice among all ranks. Calvin keeps to the first sense, that this is not common fornication but the violating of faith pledged to God, since faith and sincerity of heart constitute spiritual chastity before him.

The oven is worked three ways. Ellicott would render it, ceaseth heating from the kneading of the dough till its leavening, and explains that the baker is unremitting in keeping up the heat, the smouldering fire fed on dung and the like fuel, except when he must prepare the dough; an apt image, he says, of the incessant burning rage of lust and violence. Calvin presses his point again, that the people were corrupted not by an outward impulse but by their own inclination and a mad desire of acting wickedly, and that the fire was not suddenly lighted but had long gathered strength; the ungodly restrain their desires while no occasion offers, and give vent to them when they can sin with impunity. Clarke reports a paraphrase that reads the figure politically: the king set fire to his own oven, which is his kingdom, and put leaven in his dough, then went to rest that the fire might heat the oven and the leaven raise the dough, so that the principles he introduced might infect the whole population; and what, it asks, shall become of the oven and the bread.
5:
What day is meant is guessed at, not settled. Gill allows the birthday, the coronation day, or the day the calves were set up kept as an anniversary; or the clause may be read, it is the day of our king, as the words of false prophets exciting the people to drink his health, and so leading them by intemperance into adultery. Calvin prefers the annual day of coronation, and makes the occasion the measure of the offence: it was not sinful to keep it, but the king ought to have given thanks that God had preserved the kingdom and asked the spirit of wisdom for the year to come. Instead the princes indulge excess and so overcome their king with drinking that they make him sick, until nothing royal appears in the palace, nor anything worthy of men. Keil and Delitzsch read it as the feast the king gave his nobles, on which the princes drank till they became ill with the heat of the wine, and take the last clause to mean that the king goes about with scoffers and makes himself familiar with them, the scoffers being drunkards.

Ellicott would repoint the line. Following a hint of the ancient versions he translates that the princes have begun the day of our king with the glowing of wine, the carousal commencing at an early hour, significant of monstrous excess; he hears bitterness in the pronoun our before king, calls the common English rendering inaccurate, and takes the closing words to mean the king has made common cause with scorners.

The oven returns, and Calvin insists it is not the same oven. Before it stood for the mad lust with which they burned; here for their plots and concealed frauds, and he complains that interpreters pass the change over heedlessly, as though the prophet meant one thing in both places. His picture is of a baker who closes the door of his house, lays the fire at night while nobody perceives the oven is heating, and rests securely, having stacked the wood so the fire cannot be smothered; so the people nourished their wickedness before God, evil deeds conceived by degrees over a long time before coming forth into open acts. Wesley says the same of princes hot with ambition, revenge or covetousness, who lie in wait against the life or estate of their subjects: when they have laid a plot, though they seem to sleep, the fire glows within and flames out as soon as there is opportunity. Gill makes the plot specific: heated with wine, they were ready for any wickedness, whether adultery or treason against the king they had themselves made drunk and now despised.

Ellicott reads the sleeping baker as the passion itself, some by a change of pointing reading their anger for their baker; after the carousal, he says, the conspiracy ripens with the day.

The fallen kings are counted. Clarke says there was a pitiful slaughter among the idolatrous kings of Israel, four falling within this prophet’s own time, each cut off by the man who took his place, all idolaters and all coming to an untimely death; Wesley names the same four, fallen by the conspiracy of such hot princes, and adds that not one of them feared, trusted, or worshipped God. Calvin reads the devoured judges otherwise. Some hold that the people, as if freed from all laws, had upset all order by main force, but that seems to him strained; rather the judges were devoured because the people had by their own fault made void the favour of God, whose goodness, otherwise inexhaustible, dries up when we will not let it approach. The removal of kings and judges was no obscure sign of displeasure, a trial whether the disease was healable; it effected nothing, and the body was left mangled, as if the head had been taken from it.
8:
How the mixing was done Gill sets out in a list: locally, by dwelling among them; carnally, by intermarrying contrary to the command; civilly, by alliances and confederacies; or morally, by learning their manners and conforming to their customs, especially in religious things. He reports and sets aside a reading that makes the mixing a punishment already inflicted, the people carried captive among the nations. Henry keeps to the sin: they went up and down among the nations to beg help of one against another, when, had they kept close to God, they would have needed the help of none. Calvin presses the election: the calling of God brings holiness with it, and it was not to be endured that Ephraim, on whom God had engraven the mark of his choice, should be entangled in the superstitions of the Gentiles.

The cake is explained before it is applied. Clarke describes the baking: having heated the hearth they sweep one corner, lay the cake on it and cover it with embers, turning and covering it again until it is sufficiently baked. Henry and Wesley take the figure for divided allegiance, burnt on one side and dough on the other, good for nothing on either; Henry recalls a reign in which they halted between God and Baal, and says it is sad how many who profess religion are made up of contraries, always in one extreme or the other.

Calvin gives the figure a proverbial turn. Ephraim was in nothing fixed, as we say of a man not consistent with himself that he is neither flesh nor fish. They boasted themselves a people sacred to God, and circumcision seemed to make some difference; but the worship was corrupted and the sacrifices adulterated, so that their whole religion was a chaos of Gentile superstitions and of something resembling legitimate worship. Ellicott reads the cake as ruin rather than inconstancy: Ephraim was consumed by the unhallowed fire of a foreign worship, burnt to a cinder on one side and on the other left unfit for food, so that foreign idolatries and alliances are the ruin of the nation.

Who the strangers were history answers. Gill offers the Syrians, who in one reign made them like the dust by threshing, or the Assyrians, first a king who exacted a thousand talents of silver, and then another who took their fortified places and carried the inhabitants captive. Ellicott refers the past tense to those invasions, and says both Egypt and Assyria had come to regard Israel as the earthen pot among iron ones. Henry divides the devouring in two, some by open wars and some by pretended treaties of amity, under which they extorted wealth and made them pay dearly for what did them no good; those who do not make God their strength, he adds, make that their strength which strangers soon devour.

The grey hairs are symptoms nobody reads. Henry calls them the marks of a state waxing old and ready to vanish, and the effect of trouble, since care turns a man grey. Ellicott says the signs of senility are upon him, that grey hairs are his passing bell, and that he is under sentence of death and knows it not. Clarke compares a silly old man, nearly bald and the rest of his hair grey, who makes no provision for the eternity on whose brink he stands but calls in doctors to cure him of old age and death, and says he sees such conduct daily. Calvin makes the insensibility the worst sign: when God prevails nothing by his word or by his stripes, the sins have rooted too deep to be torn away. They felt their evils, no doubt, but did not consider the cause; and when a man cries only on account of the strokes and regards not the hand of the striker, there is complete stupidity in him.
10:
Pride is here made a witness. Gill notes the incongruity: in a weak and declining state they were proud and haughty, conceited of their safe condition and insolent towards God; their pride was so notorious that they could not deny it, and stood self-convicted. Calvin observes that the Hebrew word means both to testify and to humble, and that both senses fit; he makes little of the choice, since the design is the same either way. God had so openly chastised them that they must have perceived his hand unless blind indeed, and being warned they ought to have humbled themselves. However fiercely they rose against him and excused their sins, it availed nothing: their own pride cast them down, so that the Lord held them convicted, as though the crime had been proved by many witnesses and the mask taken away.

That they did not return Calvin will not put to ignorance. They were wholly taken up with the multitude of their deities and had no regard for God; and since he had made himself plainly known by his law, the failure to return was not error but a diabolical madness, as though they wished of their own accord to perish. God calls himself the God of Israel here, he notes, not for honour but to expose their ingratitude.

The dove is drawn from life. Gill says it picks up the corns that lie scattered and does not know the net is spread for it; when its young are taken it is unconcerned and keeps its nest in the same place; and when frightened it flies not to its dove house but about, and becomes a prey. So Ephraim, going to Egypt and Assyria for help, was ensnared, not having sense enough to see that this would be their ruin, and though they had suffered by them before, still continued their addresses. Clarke adds that the bird is easily snared and careless of its own young, and remarks that those who are themselves without heart have made it the symbol of conjugal affection, than which nothing worse could be chosen, since the dove and its mate are continually quarrelling. Wesley finds it like the dove in weakness and fear as well as imprudence, without discretion or courage.

Keil and Delitzsch narrow the comparison by rejecting two readings of it. The point is not that the dove has missed its resting place and goes fluttering about, nor that in escaping the hawk it flies into the net of the fowler, but that while flying about in search of food it does not observe the net spread for it. They take the words without heart as a predicate of Ephraim rather than a description of the dove.

The errand makes the folly plain. Clarke points out that the two courts were rivals, so Israel could not attach itself to one without incurring the jealousy of the other, and like the silly dove they fell constantly into snares: by the one betrayed, by the other ruined. Ellicott finds a definite political allusion, in a usurper who took the throne after a murder and purchased recognition by a large present to the Assyrian monarch while secretly coquetting with Egypt; the alliance that ruined Israel he places later, and notes that many commentators refer the verse to an earlier reign. For without heart he would read, without understanding. Calvin turns it into a warning about simplicity: the virtue is commendable when joined to prudence, but when men are too credulous and void of judgment it is mere folly, opposed to the knowledge God had offered in his law. He had never ceased to guide Israel by sound doctrine and had always held out the torch of his word, and yet they gave heed to the delusions of Satan and of the world; men are not to be excused by the pretext of simplicity.
12:
The net is set where the bird means to land. Clarke says God will cause them to be taken by the very people in whom they trusted, and that they shall no sooner set off for this foreign help than the net will bring them down, the allusion to the dove and to the taking of fowls being still carried on. Ellicott would render it, whenever they go, and says the ruin produced by this policy of dependence on foreign states was foreseen even then, and portrayed as a net snaring the unwary bird. Wesley puts it shortly, that though they attempt to fly they shall fall as fowls in the net; Gill notes only that the going is to Egypt or Assyria.

Calvin makes the verse a lesson about counsel. If the dove sees only the lure and does not shun the danger, it is proof of foolish simplicity; so God undertakes to disappoint all their endeavours and make their hopes vain. From this Calvin draws a rule: the issue will always be unhappy if we attempt anything contrary to the word of the Lord, or hold consultations over which his Spirit does not preside. When God is opposed to our designs, whatever we attain will at length be turned to our ruin. As he leads his own by his extended hand and gives his angels charge to guide them, so he has his expanded net for all who wander after their own erratic imaginations.

The bringing down is timed to the height of the flight. Presumptuous men are elated until they seem as though they would break through the clouds; so, Calvin has God say, I will allow them to be carried up for a time, but when they reach the clouds I will draw them down and make them know their flying avails nothing. Who would have thought so much protection lay in Assyria or Egypt? But the Lord laughs that vain power to scorn.

What the assembly had heard is read three ways. Clarke takes it of their solemn assemblies, where they had heard the law read and wrath denounced against idolaters, and reports a rendering that turns the clause round, so that God chastises them when they hearken to their assembly and take their elders counsel to go down to Egypt. Ellicott would read, according to the report to their assembly, that is, what they hear, perhaps from the prophet himself, and finds the threatenings of the law echoed here. Wesley refers the hearing simply to the prophets God had sent them.

The last verse turns on a single tense. Gill takes the fleeing plainly: they had deserted the temple and set up calves at Dan and Bethel, and instead of fleeing to God in distress fled further off, out of their own land. Keil and Delitzsch note that the word used is the one for the flying of birds, pointing back to the figures just employed, and deny that the next verb can refer to the redemption out of Egypt, since it does not stand for the preterite; they take it as voluntative, I would redeem them, but they speak lies concerning me. Ellicott renders it the same way, though I would fain redeem them, an impressive picture of the insults offered to long-suffering divine love. Calvin defends the past tense against both that reading and a question, shall I redeem them; the change of tenses was familiar to the Hebrews, and the sense is that God had often delivered them from death, and they neither changed their disposition nor gave him the praise due, so that nothing now remains but that he must destroy them. Clarke says the lies were representing God as rigorous and cruel and his service as painful; Wesley, that they belied his corrections as undeserved and the good he did as too little, or as done by their idol.
14:
The complaint is not that they were silent but that the noise was not prayer. Gill grants that in their distress they cried to the Lord, said they repented and made a show of worship, but their hearts and their mouths did not go together, so that it was not reckoned prayer at all, but only howling. Clarke puts the answer in the mouth of God: I know they cried, yea howled, but could I hear when all was forced and hypocritical, and not one sigh came from the heart? Ellicott draws the line sharply: God discriminates between a heart-cry to him and a howl of despair resembling the yell of a wild beast, and a howl upon a bed is not a sob of true repentance.

Calvin makes calling upon God the test. It is the chief exercise of religion and the thing in which repentance especially shows itself, and the outward act without the heart is only a profanation of the name of God. He allows that some worship had always remained among them, but they blended it with their own inventions, and these fictitious invocations God could not endure. On the howling he offers two constructions. The particle may be adversative, so that though grief urges them to make great noises they are mute as to any cry of prayer; or causal, which he prefers, so that the howling is why they cannot be said to cry, uttering their noise like brute animals without reason. So the unbelieving dread the mention of God, and pour forth their feelings while shunning access to him.

Why they assembled is disputed. Ellicott reports the common rendering, that they gathered to supplicate for fruitful harvests; another that they excited themselves with dervish-like devices and cries; and a third, from the ancient version and a different reading found in some manuscripts, that they cut themselves, which he thinks not improbably the right one. The charge either way is that their simulated penitence was to secure physical comforts, not to show conformity with the divine will. Clarke says shortly that in dearth and famine they call and howl, but assemble not to seek God but to invoke their false gods for corn and wine; Wesley locates the assembly in the houses of their idols.

The last verse turns on one verb, and no two read it alike. Keil and Delitzsch say it is not to chastise here but to instruct, and take the arms as object of both verbs: instructing the arms is showing where and how strength is to be acquired, and the Lord did not stop there but strengthened them too, giving power to fight and victory over their foes. Ellicott agrees that it should be instructed, God having imparted skill and power to fight their enemies. Calvin will have neither. Since the word sometimes means to bind, that seems the fitter metaphor, and chastising in no way suitable to the context: the strength of the arm depends on the structure of the nerves, and unless the bones were bound together by them a dissolution would follow. God is a surgeon here rather than a teacher, binding an arm that might otherwise have broken.

What God did for them history supplies. Gill points to a reign in which their arms were broken by the Syrians, and to two later reigns in which cities were retaken and the border restored; and since this was done by the blessing of providence, the Lord is said to have done it himself. He reports also the rendering, though I have chastised, I have strengthened them. Wesley keeps the surgery, that God bound up a broken member when their enemies had broken it, and says the mischief was devised against his prophets. Clarke will not distinguish the dealings: whether God dealt in judgment or in mercy it was all one, for in all circumstances they rebelled.
16:
Where they returned to is the first question. Gill answers it two ways: to Egypt and not to Jerusalem, to their idols and not to him whose name alone is Jehovah; or, taking the words as not on high, upwards, above, their desires were not after things above, and they looked not upward for help but to men and things on earth. He grants that they made some feint of returning, but says they presently fell back and never went on to a thorough reformation. Calvin knows an exposition that supplies something after the particle, so that they return but not for anything, and a man inquiring what was in their minds would find mere form; but he calls that strained, and holds the context requires the word to stand for God. Hypocrites, when the hand of God presses hard on them, seem different from what they were, yet always shun him, going astray by devious windings and never keeping the straight course.

The bow is explained from the workshop. Clarke says the eastern bow stands at rest in a curve and must be bent back the opposite way to be strung, which requires both strength and skill; if it is not properly done it springs back to its former position, and in the recoil endangers the archer and may even break an arm. He adds that he has been in this danger himself, and that for want of this knowledge not one commentator has hit the meaning.

Calvin takes the same figure from the other end. Some render the words the bow of darting or shooting, and the root does mean to dart; but that sense cannot stand here, since what the prophet has in view is that they put on a guise and did nothing but deceive. An archer levels at a mark, and the arrow seems directed where his eye is fixed; but if the bow is oblique the arrow flies elsewhere, or the bow may slip and throw it back at the archer. So hypocrites seem to strive with great effort, and yet their mind is driven back, and by tortuous windings they go astray and never come to God, but turn their backs on him. Wesley says the same more shortly: though they seemed bent for the mark, like a weak bow they carried not the arrow home and like a false bow never carried it straight. Ellicott puts the fault in the string: religious observance has the appearance of a bow with the arrow on it, apparently aimed at some object, but the string being slack the aim is diverted.

Why the princes are named Calvin explains as a figure of speech. He denounces vengeance again so they might feel assured the heavenly decree of their destruction could not be changed, since hypocrites, though they can hope nothing from God, never cease to flatter themselves and contrive some new hope. In saying princes the prophet takes a part for the whole; God does not threaten them as though he meant to except the common people, but implies that the destruction would be common to all, and that not even the princes would escape.

The last clause turns the boasting into the punishment. Clarke sets the two enragements against each other: their tongue was enraged against God, and the sword shall be enraged against them; they mocked him, and their fall is now a subject of derision in the land of Egypt, so that what they sowed they now reap. Ellicott makes the raving insolence of the tongue particular, taking it for boasts made of the friendship of the king of Egypt, who made Israel his tool, so that in that very land they would become objects of derision. Wesley keeps it general, that the rage was against God, his prophets and his providence, and that they shall be upbraided with it.
